tagline.text: Blue pools and a small cave behind the falls in a Siniloan forest gorge

location.label: Location
location.text: Magsaysay, Siniloan, Laguna (on foot from the Trekkers area at Km 17–18 of the Siniloan–Famy–Infanta road)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱500–800 (per person, day trip from Manila)

children.text: A multi-tiered waterfall hidden in a forest gorge in Siniloan, at the eastern tip of Laguna, known for its blue-green pool and a small cave behind the upper falls. It can be done as a day trip by bus from Manila, on a guided trek that crosses several streams.

Asul na Talon Falls is a waterfall deep in the hills of Barangay Magsaysay in Siniloan, at the far eastern end of Laguna province. In Filipino, asul means blue and talon means waterfall, so the name means "Blue Falls." Follow the Siniloan–Famy–Infanta road toward Quezon province, then enter the forest on foot from the Trekkers registration post at Km 17 or from a trailhead near Km 18. Unlike popular tourist waterfalls near Manila such as Pagsanjan Falls, this is a quiet gorge waterfall with almost no facilities.

The name comes from the deep pool beneath the falls. According to several travel accounts, it is less that the stream itself is blue and more that the basin where the water lands looks blue-green. One blogger noted that the water is not actually blue, while another wrote of clear blue water, so the impression can change with the weather and water volume on the day you visit. The depth of the pool is unknown, and one blogger reported failing several times to measure it, so treat it as water of unknown depth and enter with care.

The falls do not drop in a single stream but flow in several tiers among large boulders. Accounts describe passing a small unnamed lower fall (under about 10 feet) before reaching Asul na Talon, and a taller upper fall (at least about 15 feet) farther up. There is a small cave behind the upper fall that is known as a photo spot, but reaching it reportedly means climbing a nearly vertical, slippery rock face. This is not a place that wows with height, so you may be disappointed if you expect a big waterfall; it suits people who enjoy walking a stream and its rocks and water.

The trek generally goes like this. Starting from the road, you walk across flat grass and forest trail, cross streams, push through mud and brush past the small lower fall, and then climb against the current over boulders to reach Asul na Talon. Accounts put the walk from the road to the falls at about
30 minutes to 1 hour 30 minutes

, which varies a lot with the starting point, your pace, and the water level. One account spent nearly 30 minutes pushing through undergrowth and then about 10 more minutes walking, while another took 20–25 minutes to the first fall and under 10 minutes from there. The last stretch is a climb up slippery rocks against the current, so you will use your hands a lot and it is easier with a light pack. It is safer, and much easier to find the way, with a local guide rather than going alone. Access routes differ slightly between accounts. One account entered the grass and forest behind a house at Km 18, while another set out with a guide from the Trekkers registration post. A 2021 account said the falls are right beside a farm in Siniloan. Because there is no single fixed route, it is safest to decide which way to go with the registration post or a local guide. The falls are commonly combined in one day with nearby Hagdang Bato Falls, Tulay na Bato Falls, and the Kabagan waterfall cavern. Most of the fees and rules here come from travel accounts written between 2013 and 2021, so check the latest situation before you go.

The pool beneath the falls looks blue-green, which is said to be the origin of the name. Accounts mention that you can swim there, but the depth is unknown, so check conditions with your guide before getting in.
Water drops several times among big boulders, which makes for good photos. The look changes a lot between days with more and less water.
A small cave behind the upper fall is known as a photo spot. You have to cross a nearly vertical, slippery rock face, so check your footwear and condition and do not push yourself.
You walk through grass and forest and cross streams two or more times. The trail has lots of mud and wet rock, which makes the trek fun.
The usual plan is to walk on from Asul na Talon to Kabagan, Hagdang Bato, and Tulay na Bato Falls, in that order. Some people walk it in reverse.
It takes about 3 hours by bus from Manila to reach the Trekkers area, so an early-morning start makes a day trip possible.

children.text: Take a bus toward Infanta from the Raymond bus terminal at Legarda in Manila. Tell the driver in advance that you are getting off at Km 17 "Trekkers."
Arrive at Trekkers and
register and get a guide assigned

Walk the forest trail with your guide. Grass, muddy sections, and stream crossings follow, and you pass a small unnamed waterfall.
Arrive at Asul na Talon, look around the blue pool and the tiered falls, and take photos. Decide on the upper fall and the cave depending on the condition of the rocks.
Depending on your schedule and stamina, continue to Kabagan, Hagdang Bato, or Tulay na Bato Falls, or return the same way.
Return to Trekkers, wash up, change clothes, and take a bus back to Manila at around 4 PM.

Visit other falls such as Hagdang Bato or Tulay na Bato, then return to Manila by an afternoon bus.

Because this is a gorge waterfall, it is safest to avoid going during or right after rain. Travel accounts say that in the rainy season the streams swell and are hard to cross, leeches are plentiful, and the trail turns muddy.

The most comfortable period is the drier months of March to May. It is hot then, so a swim in the cool pool is most welcome. Rain is still possible from December to February because of the northeast monsoon, so check the weather before you leave.
Arriving early on a weekday morning lets you enjoy the place in relative quiet. One account advised against visiting in the rainy season.

There is no proper lodging inside the trekking area. Most people make it a day trip from Manila, and anyone who wants to stay overnight has to look for small accommodations in Siniloan or Famy town. Check rates and whether they are open locally.

There are also no restaurants on the trekking route, so bring packed lunch, water, and snacks. One travel account said the group had lunch at a restaurant in Famy before heading on. Some accounts say stream water along the trail can be used as drinking water, but bring plenty of water if you can.

Siniloan town has small eateries and a market where you can grab a simple meal on the way back. After the trek, bring a towel and spare clothes so that you can change into them near the registration post.
Register at the Trekkers registration post and move with a guide. Accounts say you cannot go into the hills without one.
To deal with leeches (limatik), bring long socks, insect repellent, and salt.
The route is wet, so non-slip water shoes or trekking sandals are best.
Put your clothes, phone, and wallet in a waterproof bag or plastic bags.
Accounts say phone signal is weak, so save maps and contacts in advance.
The cave behind the falls requires climbing slippery rock, so do not push yourself and follow your guide's judgment.
Plan to be back at the registration post by 3–4 PM so that you do not miss the bus back to Manila.
Carry out all your trash. One account says the landowner complained about litter.
Accounts say people stayed at the falls for about 15 minutes. Start early if you want more time for photos and swimming.
When crossing streams, follow the guide and step on the rocks the guide steps on.
Do not go during or right after rain. The streams can rise suddenly and the rocks become very slippery.
The depth of the pool is unknown, so do not enter deep water without a life jacket.
The rock leading to the cave behind the upper fall is reportedly nearly vertical and slippery. Do not climb it if you are not confident.
Accounts mention thorny plants and mud on the grassy trail and horse droppings in some sections.
Accounts say the area is a protected area that includes private land, so do not enter without permission.
Fees, registration rules, and trail conditions can change. Check the latest notices with the Siniloan tourism office or the registration post before you leave.
